title: The empty circle
hook: eighth picture: both ox and self forgotten, an empty circle

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seventh picture: home, the ox forgotten, the man resting in the sun. Your line: the ox forgotten. What did you let be easy, without checking? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-eight.

Turn the page to the eighth picture and there's nothing on it. No herdsman. No ox. No hut, no field, no rope. Just a circle, drawn in ink, with empty paper inside. For seven pictures we've followed a man and an animal through grass and mud and weather. Yesterday the ox dropped out of the frame and the man stayed. Now he's gone too. It can look as if a page went missing at the printer. It didn't. Today: the empty circle.
screen: `NO HERDSMAN. NO OX.` → `JUST A CIRCLE OF INK.` → `NOTHING MISSING.`

segments.voice: First, both are forgotten. The Chinese title of this picture says it directly: person and ox, both forgotten. The verse, in paraphrase, lists them as they go: whip, rope, person, ox, all gone into emptiness. Yesterday the herdsman let go of the thing he was chasing. Today he lets go of himself as the one who chased it. Second, no place to stand. The preface, in paraphrase, says he doesn't linger where there is awakening, and passes quickly by where there is none. He doesn't settle into either one. That's why the eye can't find him. It isn't that he vanished. It's that there's no fixed spot left to point at and say, there he is, the enlightened man. Third, no praise can reach it. The preface mentions birds bringing flowers, an old story of a hermit so holy that birds brought him offerings, and says that kind of praise would mean nothing here. The verse adds an image: the sky is too vast for anyone to survey; a snowflake can't fall on a blazing furnace. Even the idea of being special melts. Fourth, why a circle. An empty frame could look like loss. But a circle is whole, unbroken, closed. In Japanese Zen, drawing a circle in a single brushstroke, the enso, became its own practice, a way of showing the mind at the moment of the stroke. In this picture the emptiness isn't a blank where something used to be. It's the paper the whole story was drawn on. The herdsman, the ox and the search all happened inside it, and it's still here when they're gone.
screen: `PERSON AND OX, BOTH FORGOTTEN.` · `NO PLACE LEFT TO STAND.` · `NO PRAISE CAN REACH IT.` · `A CIRCLE IS WHOLE.` · then, large: `THE EMPTY CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. If there's paper and a pen nearby, draw a circle, once, in one movement. If not, trace one slowly in the air with a finger. Don't fix it. Wobbly is fine; it's yours. Then set the pen down and look at the inside of the circle. Empty, and nothing missing. Let the breath come and go inside it. If thoughts appear, let them be drawn and fade on the same paper. The bell holds the time.
The empty circle. The eighth oxherding picture: ox and self both forgotten, a single circle with nothing inside, whole and unbroken. Today's word.

Your line: the empty circle. Today, when you catch yourself keeping score of how well you're doing, picture the circle and drop the scorekeeper for a breath. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: In Zen, the eighth oxherding picture is drawn as an empty circle, and in Japanese Zen the enso, a circle brushed in one stroke, is practiced and hung in temples and homes as an expression of the mind at that moment.

original.note: Chinese (renniu juwang): 'person and ox both forgotten', the name of the eighth oxherding picture.

trapdoor: what you thought: an empty circle means nothing is there.
what it means: ox and self both forgotten; a whole, unbroken circle with nothing missing.
what a scholar hears: the preface says he lingers neither in awakening nor outside it, so no eye can find him and no praise can reach him.

notes: All oxherding material paraphrased. Check: verse (whip, rope, person, ox all merge in emptiness; sky so vast no message can stain it; snowflake in a fire); preface (seeks no awakening, does not stay where there is none; birds bringing flowers would be meaningless praise).
The birds-with-flowers allusion is described generally as 'an old story of a hermit'; tradition links it to the Chan monk Niutou Farong. Not named in voice; confirm.
Enso described as becoming its own practice in Japanese Zen; no dates or names given.
'It can look as if a page went missing' is a light illustrative aside, not a claim; cut if Keeper prefers.
Original 人牛俱忘; pronunciation approximates Mandarin renniu juwang.
Editor: preface paraphrase corrected (he does not linger where there is awakening and passes by where there is none); verse image reworded away from a modern copyrighted translation's wording.
